documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT

David is 57, here to establish. His previous internist retired and he did not take to the group that absorbed the panel. Works as a project manager, hybrid, desk-heavy.

Hypertension: told he had high pressure in his mid-40s. Has been on lisinopril 10 and amlodipine 5 for several years. Home cuff readings he describes as "all over the place," some 130s, some 150s. Admits he misses a dose here and there when traveling for work. No headaches, chest pain, palpitations or leg swelling.

Kidneys: in 2019 the old office told him his kidney function was reduced and put it down to blood pressure. Says he had an ultrasound then that was fine. No nephrologist. Avoids ibuprofen since then, uses acetaminophen for the odd backache.

PMH: hypertension; CKD stage 3 (hypertensive per prior office).
PSH: none.
Meds: lisinopril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily.
Allergies: none known.
FH: father had high blood pressure and a heart attack at 67. Mother type 2 diabetes, stroke at 72. One brother with high blood pressure. Nobody with dementia, motor neuron disease or bowel tumors that he knows of.
SH: married, lives with his wife. Smoked about a pack a day for 20 years, stopped in 2014. Rare drink, one or two a month. No drugs.
Screening: colonoscopy 2019 at the old office, told normal.

ROS: negative except as above.

Exam: BP 146/92 (repeat similar), see vitals. Well appearing, overweight. Neck supple, no thyroid enlargement, no bruits. Heart regular, S1 S2 normal, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, no masses, no bruit. No edema. Pulses 2+ throughout. Neuro grossly intact.

A/P
1. Essential hypertension, above goal today. He is honest about missed doses. Same regimen for now, home log twice daily for two weeks and send it in. Low-salt diet reviewed.
2. CKD 3 by history. CMP, urine albumin/creatinine today. Keep avoiding NSAIDs. Records from prior office requested.
3. Former smoker, 20 pack-years, quit 7 years ago. Qualifies for lung screening; discussed what it can and can't find and the chance of a false alarm. He wants it. Low-dose CT ordered.
4. Health maintenance: CBC, lipids, TSH, hep C and HIV screens with today's blood. Flu shot and pneumococcal vaccine at a nurse visit next month when the flu shot arrives.

Follow up 3 months.

documents.title: Records request
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Signed release on file. Request faxed to prior internal medicine office for notes, labs and imaging 2016 to present.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi David, your labs are back. Kidney function is reduced, creatinine 1.74, which puts the filtration rate in the mid 40s. That fits what your old office described, and now we have our own starting point to follow. There is a small amount of protein (albumin) in the urine, 72, which is common with blood-pressure-related kidney disease and one more reason to get the pressure down. Potassium, blood count, cholesterol, thyroid all fine. Hep C and HIV screens negative. Keep the home log going. Talk soon.

documents.title: Prior internal medicine records (summary)
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Outside records received from prior internist, 38 pages, scanned to media.

Reviewed:
- Hypertension on problem list since 2009. Lisinopril and amlodipine in place since at least 2016.
- Creatinine rose into the 1.6 to 1.7 range in 2019; CKD stage 3 entered, felt to be hypertensive nephrosclerosis. No nephrology referral.
- Renal ultrasound 2019: both kidneys normal in size, no hydronephrosis, no stones or masses.
- Screening colonoscopy 2019: normal to the cecum, no polyps, repeat at 10 years.
- Tobacco history consistent with what he gave us.
Nothing that changes the plan.

ANNUAL EXAM, age 58

Interval: appendectomy in January, recovered. Working full time. Walks the dog most evenings. No complaints today.

Meds: lisinopril 10, amlodipine 5. NKDA.

ROS: no chest pain, no palpitations, no shortness of breath, no change in bowels, no urinary symptoms.

Exam: as charted vitals. HEENT normal. Neck no nodes, thyroid normal. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, healed RLQ scar, no hernia felt. No edema. Skin no concerning lesions. Neuro nonfocal.

Plan:
- HTN: borderline-high again. Same meds, he is keeping a log.
- CKD 3b: CMP and urine albumin today.
- Lipids, CBC.
- Flu and bivalent COVID booster today.
- Colon screening up to date (2019). Lung screen due again in winter.
- PHQ-2 negative.

documents.title: Primary Care Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: getting winded.

HPI: Over about two months he notices he gets out of breath on the stairs to his office and on the hill on his dog walk, which never used to bother him. Seems to be getting a bit worse. Settles quickly with rest. No chest pain or pressure, no palpitations, no lightheadedness or fainting. No cough, no fever. Sleeps flat on one pillow. No ankle swelling. Has not checked BP in a couple of weeks.

Exam: BP 158/96 left arm seated, repeat 156/94. Sat normal at rest. Comfortable talking. JVP not elevated. Heart regular, S1 S2, no murmur or gallop. Lungs clear throughout. No edema. Calves soft.

A/P: Exertional dyspnea in a man with years of suboptimally controlled hypertension and CKD, family history of early-ish MI in his father. Need to look at the heart. Referring to cardiology for evaluation and echo; they can decide on any stress testing. Go to the ED for chest pain, breathlessness at rest or fainting. Same BP meds until he's seen.

events.reason: Worsening shortness of breath on exertion

reports.text: Complete 2D, M-mode and Doppler study. Left ventricle: normal chamber size, LV internal diameter in diastole 4.9 cm. Increased wall thickness, interventricular septum 1.4 cm and posterior wall 1.3 cm, concentric. LVEF 60% by biplane method, no regional wall motion abnormality. Mitral inflow and tissue Doppler show an impaired relaxation pattern consistent with reduced LV compliance. Right ventricle normal size and function. Atria normal size. Aortic, mitral, tricuspid and pulmonic valves structurally normal without stenosis or regurgitation. Aortic root normal. No pericardial effusion.
reports.conclusion: Left ventricular hypertrophy with reduced compliance (impaired relaxation), normal LV size and systolic function, LVEF 60%. No valvular disease.

documents.title: Cardiology consultation (received)
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside cardiology group
Date of service: 11/04/2022

Thank you for the referral of Mr. Donovan, 58, for exertional breathlessness.

History: Over roughly two months, progressive breathlessness climbing stairs and walking uphill, improving with rest. Denies angina, palpitations, presyncope, orthopnea or edema. Long history of hypertension with uneven control. CKD stage 3 per PCP. Former smoker, 20 pack-years, quit 2014. Father with hypertension and MI at 67.

Medications: lisinopril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily. Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: BP 168/96. Regular rhythm. PMI palpable and displaced laterally. S1 and S2 normal, no murmur, rub or gallop. Lungs clear. No JVD, no peripheral edema.

Data: Recent labs reviewed: electrolytes and blood count normal, creatinine at his known CKD baseline.
Echocardiogram today: thickened LV walls with reduced compliance, normal cavity size, preserved systolic function (EF 60%), no valve disease.

Impression: Left ventricular hypertrophy from long-standing hypertension, with reduced LV compliance, which I suspect accounts for his exertional symptoms. No evidence of valvular disease or systolic dysfunction.

Recommendations: blood pressure control is the main treatment for the hypertrophy; continue current regimen and follow with primary care. Return to cardiology as needed.

Outside cardiology consultant

orders.reason: Postprandial diarrhea with flushing and weight loss

documents.title: Primary Care Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: GI symptoms x ~3 months.

HPI: Since around January, episodes of nausea, crampy lower and mid abdominal pain and watery diarrhea, mostly within an hour of meals, several days a week. During some episodes his face and neck go warm and red for a few minutes; his wife has seen it. No blood or black stool, no vomiting, no fever. No travel, no antibiotics, nobody sick at home. Weight 86 kg at his physical, 81.5 today, so about 10 lb in the last two months without trying. Appetite ok.

Exam: weight as charted. Not toxic. Abdomen soft, mild diffuse tenderness without guarding, normal bowel sounds, healed RLQ scar. Liver edge not clearly felt by me. No rash.

A/P: Postprandial diarrhea with episodic flushing and real weight loss in a 59-year-old. Infection unlikely with this time course. Flushing with diarrhea raises concern for a hormone-secreting tumor among other things; colonoscopy 2019 was normal. Referring to GI urgently for workup; they will likely want imaging and urine studies. CMP, CBC today. Diet diary meanwhile.

events.reason: Diarrhea, flushing, weight loss (ordered by gastroenterology)

reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
reports.text: Technique: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast (reduced dose for renal function) and oral contrast. Findings: A 4.0 cm enhancing soft tissue mass arises from the distal ileum. Three hypervascular lesions in the liver, the largest 1.8 cm in the right lobe. Spleen, pancreas, adrenal glands normal. Kidneys symmetric in size without hydronephrosis. No ascites. No bowel obstruction. Appendix surgically absent. Bladder and prostate unremarkable. No suspicious osseous lesions. Lung bases clear.
reports.conclusion: 4.0 cm distal ileal mass with three hypervascular liver lesions (largest 1.8 cm), consistent with a primary ileal neuroendocrine tumor with hepatic metastases.

conditions.label: Malignant carcinoid tumor of the ileum

documents.title: Gastroenterology consultation (received)
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Outside gastroenterology practice
Visit 05/08/2023

Reason for referral: three months of meal-related nausea, cramping and watery diarrhea with flushing; weight loss.

History: Symptoms several times weekly, typically after eating, at times with warmth and redness of the face. About 10 lb lost over two months unintentionally. No recent travel, antibiotic exposure or ill contacts. Seen by cardiology six months ago for LVH. Hypertension, CKD stage 3. Open appendectomy 2022.
Medications: lisinopril 10 mg, amlodipine 5 mg. NKDA.
Former smoker, 20 pack-years. Rare alcohol.

Exam: Appears well nourished despite the weight loss. Abdomen soft; liver edge palpable, mildly enlarged. Rectal: brown stool, guaiac negative. Skin without rash.

Studies:
- 24-hour urine 5-HIAA 38 mg/24 h (elevated).
- Niacin level mildly low.
- CT abdomen/pelvis 05/02: 4.0 cm distal ileal mass, three hypervascular liver lesions (largest 1.8 cm, right lobe).

Assessment: Carcinoid syndrome due to a small bowel (ileal) neuroendocrine tumor with liver metastases. Mild niacin deficiency fits tryptophan diversion by the tumor.

Plan: Referred to surgical oncology regarding resection of the primary and to medical oncology for somatostatin analog therapy and ongoing care. Will send tissue-confirmed staging once available. Copy to PCP.

Outside gastroenterology consultant

documents.title: Call with patient and wife
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: GI letter in today. Called David, his wife on speaker. He already heard the diagnosis from GI last week. Went over it in plain terms: slow-growing neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumor in the small bowel with spots in the liver; the flushing and diarrhea are from hormones it makes. Surgical oncology appointment is next week, oncology after. They asked good questions about what metastatic means here; I said this tumor type often behaves very slowly and oncology will give them specifics. Offered a visit any time. They know how to reach me.

documents.title: Spouse call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Wife called (on HIPAA form). David had his surgery on 6/19 at the regional hospital, a big midline incision; they took out the tumor with part of the small bowel and the right side of the colon. Home since Saturday 6/24. Walking, eating soft food, bowels moving, pain controlled with tylenol. No fever. Staples came out before discharge. She did not get any papers for us. Booked post-op visit 7/6 with PCP. Records request sent to hospital.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Post-hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen 2.5 weeks after exploratory laparotomy with ileal resection and right hemicolectomy (6/19, regional hospital; we still have no op note or discharge summary, requested again).

Per patient and wife: surgeon took the small bowel tumor and the right colon; the liver spots were left, to be treated with medicine through oncology. First oncology visit is 7/18.

Feels tired but better each day. Eating small meals. Stools 2-3 a day, looser than normal, less cramping than before surgery. Still some flushing. No fever, no vomiting, no wound drainage. Pain mild.

Exam: weight as charted, down a bit more since April. Midline incision healing well, no erythema or drainage. Old RLQ scar flat. Abdomen soft, appropriately tender near the incision. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Calves soft.

A/P
1. S/p laparotomy, ileal resection and right hemicolectomy for ileal neuroendocrine tumor. Recovering as expected. Lifting limit per surgery.
2. Metastatic carcinoid with carcinoid syndrome: oncology next.
3. HTN: acceptable today, same meds.
4. CKD 3b: BMP today after surgery and contrast.

documents.title: Specialty pharmacy
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Specialty pharmacy called asking for clinicals for a prior auth on Sandostatin LAR 30 mg every 4 weeks. Prescriber is the oncologist, not us. Gave them the oncology office as the contact and faxed our last note and the GI letter at their request. Not on our med list yet; flagged for PCP.

reports.text: Specimen: terminal ileum and right colon, resection. Gross: segment of terminal ileum with attached cecum and ascending colon; a firm tan-yellow submucosal mass in the distal ileum measuring 4.0 cm. Microscopic: nests and trabeculae of uniform cells with round nuclei and salt-and-pepper chromatin infiltrating the bowel wall; mitoses rare; no necrosis. Immunostains: tumor cells positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin. Ki-67 proliferation index 2%. Margins: proximal, distal and radial margins negative. Lymph nodes: 0 of 14 involved. Colon otherwise unremarkable.
reports.conclusion: Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor of the ileum, grade 1 (Ki-67 2%), 4.0 cm. Margins negative. 0 of 14 lymph nodes involved.

documents.title: Pathology received
documents.author: front desk

documents.title: Medical oncology consultation (received)
documents.author: oncology
documents.body:
Outside medical oncology
Initial consultation 07/18/2023

Diagnosis: Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor of the ileum, grade 1 (Ki-67 2%), resected 06/19/2023 with negative margins and 0/14 nodes; liver metastases (three lesions, largest 1.8 cm) unresected. Carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhea), urine 5-HIAA elevated.

He is recovering from surgery, still with flushing and loose stools several times a week. Weight down about 15 lb from baseline. Performance status good.

Plan: Start octreotide LAR 30 mg IM every 4 weeks, given here, first dose today. Surveillance cross-sectional imaging in about 11 months, sooner if symptoms change. Return in 3 months.

Meds: lisinopril 10, amlodipine 5, octreotide LAR as above. NKDA.

Outside medical oncology

documents.title: General surgery consultation (received)
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
Outside general surgery clinic
Seen 01/24/2024

CC: lower abdominal bulge enlarging over 6 months.

HPI: 59-year-old man with a lump in the right lower abdomen first noticed about six months ago, slowly enlarging, more prominent with coughing or straining. No pain, nausea or obstructive symptoms. Surgical history: open appendectomy two years ago via RLQ incision; exploratory laparotomy with ileal resection and right hemicolectomy June 2023 for a neuroendocrine tumor, on octreotide through oncology. Hypertension, CKD 3, LVH.
Meds: lisinopril, amlodipine, octreotide LAR. NKDA. Former smoker.

Exam: soft, non-tender bulge in the right lower quadrant at the appendectomy scar, enlarging with straining and reducing completely when he lies supine. No overlying erythema or warmth. Midline incision intact without fascial defect on palpation.

Imaging: ultrasound 01/10 shows an anterior abdominal wall defect with protrusion of omental fat.

Assessment: Incisional hernia, right lower quadrant, reducible, asymptomatic.

Plan: Given that it contains only omentum, is painless and fully reducible, and he is still recovering from major surgery last summer, I recommend watchful waiting. Avoid heavy lifting. Return promptly for pain, a bulge that will not reduce, nausea or vomiting. Happy to revisit repair in future.

Outside general surgeon

documents.body:
CC: weak hands, tripping.

HPI: Over about six months his grip has gotten weaker. Hard to open jars, dropped his coffee mug twice, keys are fiddly. Also catches his toes and trips over his own feet, has not fallen hard. Occasional cramps in calves and forearms, and he notices little twitches in the muscles of his arms and legs. No numbness or tingling. No neck pain. Bladder and bowels unchanged. No double vision, no trouble swallowing or speaking.

Exam: thinning of the muscles between the thumb and index finger both hands, grip reduced bilaterally. Visible fasciculations over both forearms. Reflexes brisk at knees and ankles. Toe walking a bit unsteady. Light touch and vibration normal in hands and feet. Cranial nerves normal.

A/P: Progressive painless weakness with wasting, fasciculations and brisk reflexes, sensation spared. Worrying for motor neuron disease; other causes need excluding. CBC, BMP, TSH, CK today. Urgent neurology referral for evaluation and EMG. He and his wife understand we are looking for a serious diagnosis among others; did not want to say more until neurology sees him.

documents.title: Your labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi David, blood count, electrolytes and thyroid are normal; kidney numbers are where they usually are for you. The muscle enzyme (CK) is slightly up at 268, which can happen when muscles are irritated and is something neurology will want to see. Your neurology appointment is July 31. Call me any time before then.

events.reason: Progressive hand weakness and difficulty walking

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth twice daily, 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals

reports.text: Motor and sensory nerve conductions in the upper and lower limbs, and needle EMG of selected muscles in the cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral segments. Sensory responses normal in amplitude and velocity. Motor responses reduced in amplitude in the median and ulnar nerves with normal distal latencies and conduction velocities, no conduction block. Needle EMG: fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves with fasciculation potentials in multiple muscles of the cervical and lumbosacral segments and the thoracic paraspinals, with large, long-duration motor units and reduced recruitment.
reports.conclusion: Widespread active (acute) and chronic denervation with normal sensory studies, in keeping with a disorder of the motor neurons.

documents.title: Neurology consultation (received)
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
Outside neurology, neuromuscular clinic
Date of visit: 07/31/2024

Referred for progressive weakness of the hands and trouble walking.

History: About six months of declining grip strength, difficulty holding objects, frequently tripping. Cramps and twitching in arms and legs. No sensory symptoms, no bladder or bowel change. Background: hypertension, CKD stage 3, LVH, metastatic ileal neuroendocrine tumor on octreotide, incisional hernia.
Meds: lisinopril 10, amlodipine 5, octreotide LAR 30 q4wk. NKDA. Former smoker. No family history of neurodegenerative disease.

Exam: wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles bilaterally; fasciculations in both upper limbs. Lower limb reflexes brisk. Plantar response extensor on the right, flexor on the left. Sensation intact to all modalities. No bladder or bowel dysfunction reported.

Labs from PCP 06/10 reviewed: CBC, electrolytes and thyroid function normal; CK mildly elevated at 268.
EMG/NCS today: active and chronic denervation in several regions; normal sensory studies.

Impression: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, with upper and lower motor neuron signs in multiple regions and supportive electrodiagnostics.

Plan: Diagnosis discussed at length with him and his wife. Start riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Liver tests monthly for the first three months, then periodically; we would appreciate PCP drawing these. Enrollment in our multidisciplinary ALS clinic with PT, OT, speech and respiratory therapy. Return in about 6 months, sooner as needed.

Outside neurologist

documents.title: Primary Care Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Here with his wife after neurology confirmed ALS on 7/31. Long visit.

How he's doing: stunned but steady. Started riluzole 50 BID two weeks ago, mild queasiness first few days, now fine. Hands same as in June; walking same. No swallowing or speech trouble. Breathing fine lying flat.

Mood: sad, not hopeless. PHQ-9 4. Sleeping. Wife is his main support. Does not want counseling right now; knows it's available.

Exam: hand intrinsic wasting, forearm fasciculations as before. Lungs clear. Heart regular. BP as charted.

A/P:
1. ALS, new: riluzole per neurology; LFTs today and monthly x2 more, standing orders placed. ALS clinic enrollment underway.
2. Advance care planning (25 min): he named his wife as health care agent; proxy form completed and scanned. Early conversation about what matters to him (staying at home, staying clear-headed). Will revisit as things change; no decisions about breathing or feeding support yet.
3. Work: still working, will need leave paperwork at some point; bring forms.
4. HTN, CKD, carcinoid: stable, unchanged.

reports.text: Spirometry with slow vital capacity, maximal respiratory pressures and diffusing capacity. Good effort, reproducible. FVC 74% predicted. FEV1 75% predicted. FEV1/FVC 0.80. Slow vital capacity reduced. Maximal inspiratory pressure -52 cmH2O (reduced). Maximal expiratory pressure 68 cmH2O (reduced). DLCO 88% predicted.
reports.conclusion: Reduced vital capacity with a normal FEV1/FVC ratio and reduced maximal respiratory pressures, with normal diffusing capacity: pattern of respiratory muscle weakness.

documents.title: Neurology follow-up (received)
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
Outside neurology, ALS clinic
Visit 02/07/2025

Interval: Over the past six months, more trouble with buttons and with stairs; uses the railing every time. No swallowing or speech complaints. Tolerating riluzole; PCP liver tests normal. On medical leave since October.

Exam: atrophy of the hand muscles, fasciculations in the arms, hyperreflexia in the legs. Sensory examination normal.

Pulmonary function today: FVC 74% predicted, FEV1 75%, FEV1/FVC 0.80; vital capacity reduced; MIP -52 and MEP 68 cmH2O, both reduced; DLCO normal at 88%. Restrictive pattern from respiratory muscle weakness, no intrinsic lung disease.

Plan: continue riluzole 50 mg BID. Clinic PT for home exercise and fall prevention, OT for button hook and adaptive utensils. Repeat breathing tests each visit. Return 6 months.

Meds: riluzole, lisinopril, amlodipine, octreotide LAR. NKDA.
Outside neurologist

documents.title: Initial Preventive Physical Examination
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Initial preventive exam, new federal coverage through disability. Wife present.

Functional: dresses with some help for buttons, uses a button hook from OT. Bathes himself with a grab bar. Climbs stairs with the rail, slowly. No falls since we last met. Driving short distances only, wife does highway driving. Hearing and vision fine.
Cognition: intact on conversation and clock draw.
Mood: PHQ-9 4. Says the leave helped.
Home safety: rails in, bath mat, night lights. Advance directive and proxy on file from August, reviewed, unchanged.

Meds: lisinopril 10, amlodipine 5, riluzole 50 BID, octreotide LAR 30 q4wk.

Exam: BP as charted. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear, speaks full sentences. Abdomen soft, RLQ hernia reducible. Hand intrinsic wasting, forearm fasciculations. Gait cautious, broad-based. No edema.

Plan:
- HTN/LVH: fine.
- CKD 3b: creatinine drifting up slowly over the past year; CMP and urine albumin today, follow.
- ALS: neurology/ALS clinic; PT home program.
- Carcinoid: oncology, CT due June.
- Prevention: vaccines current through fall. Colon due 2029.
- Written screening schedule given.

No new liver lesions. No adenopathy, ascites or peritoneal disease. Small right lower quadrant fat-containing abdominal wall hernia, unchanged. Kidneys without hydronephrosis. Lung bases clear.
reports.conclusion: Stable hepatic metastases. No new disease.

documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
Outside neurology, ALS clinic
Visit 07/25/2025 [received after records request]

Interval: Six months of gradually harder swallowing and slurred speech; sometimes chokes on thin liquids. His wife has noticed more clumsiness and several stumbles at home. No falls with injury.

Exam: tongue wasting with fasciculations. Speech nasal and spastic. Brisk jaw jerk. Increased tone in both arms with hyperreflexia. Spastic gait with cane. No sensory loss. Cognition intact.

Labs today: CBC, electrolytes, thyroid function normal; renal function at his CKD baseline.

Speech-language pathology swallow evaluation (same day): cough with thin liquids; safe with mildly thick liquids and chin-tuck. Soft, moist diet.

Discussion: bulbar progression. We discussed a feeding tube now while breathing tests allow it; he prefers to wait and will reconsider.

Plan: continue riluzole; SLP strategies; dietitian; return 6 months.

Outside neurologist

With wife. We have no letter from the July ALS clinic visit; history from them.

Per wife: neurology said the ALS is now affecting swallowing and speech. Speech therapist watched him drink and eat, advised thickening thin liquids and tucking his chin. Feeding tube came up; David wants to hold off. Speech is slower and more nasal to me than in June. Coughs less with the thickener. Weight down 3 kg since spring.

Exam: weight as charted. Speech nasal, effortful, understandable. Lungs clear. BP fine.

A/P:
1. ALS with bulbar involvement. Weight loss; reinforced calorie-dense soft foods per dietitian. Respect his choice on the tube; he knows the window matters. Asked records for the clinic note.
2. HTN, CKD, carcinoid: stable.
Follow up 3 months, video ok.

Outside neurology, ALS clinic
Visit 01/26/2026

Interval: Six months of steadily harder stair climbing and weaker grip; occasional slurring. His wife describes shallow breathing, worse at night, and episodes of laughing or crying he cannot stop.

Exam: sensation normal. Hand muscle atrophy, fasciculations in both arms, reflexes brisk, both plantar responses extensor.

Respiratory: ABG on room air in the PFT lab pH 7.42, PaCO2 45, PaO2 70, HCO3 24. FVC 60% predicted.

With wife, in wheelchair today for the distance from the car.

ALS clinic 1/26: breathing tests down (FVC 60%, CO2 45 on the gas), BiPAP ordered for nights; machine came yesterday, first night he wore it 3 hours, then pulled it off. Wife says his breathing at night seems deeper with it on. Also told me about the laughing/crying spells neurology noted; he finds them embarrassing more than distressing.

Swallowing stable on thickened liquids. Weight down to 74. Bowels fine on octreotide.

Exam: speech slow, nasal. Breathing unlabored at rest, sat normal. Lungs clear but shallow. Heart regular. No edema. Hernia reducible.

1. ALS with respiratory involvement: BiPAP nightly, work up to full nights; RT from vendor following.
2. HTN: BP fine.
3. CKD 3b: creatinine has been creeping up; BMP today.

documents.author: nephrology
documents.body:
Outside nephrology
Follow-up 08/10/2026

62-year-old with CKD stage 3b attributed to hypertensive nephrosclerosis, seen for routine follow-up. Says he takes lisinopril and amlodipine as prescribed. Following the low-potassium diet we reviewed at his last visit. No palpitations; no weakness beyond his established ALS pattern. Uses nocturnal BiPAP.

Other history: LVH; metastatic ileal neuroendocrine tumor on octreotide; ALS on riluzole; incisional hernia.
Allergies: NKDA.

BP 132/84. Exam: no edema. Heart regular, lungs clear. Neurologic findings of ALS unchanged per patient and wife; otherwise unremarkable.

Labs today: potassium 5.6 mEq/L (H), creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (H), eGFR 35, bicarbonate 24, calcium 9.2.

Assessment: CKD 3b, slowly progressive. Hyperkalemia persisting despite dietary changes.

Plan: continue low-potassium diet. Repeat BMP in two weeks; please draw at PCP and forward. We will decide on further management with that result. Return 3 months.

Outside nephrologist
